Program, Process and Thread
Program: Executable file containing instructions to perform a task.
Compiled code stored on disk.
Process: Program that is currently under execution (in RAM).
Thread: Smallest unit of execution within a process.
Multiple threads can run concurrently inside one process.

Thread Characteristics
Thread is a lightweight process.
Represents a single sequence of execution.
Threads share memory and resources of the parent process.
Used to achieve parallelism inside applications.
Example: Browser tabs, text editor spell-checking and formatting.

Memory | Each process has separate memory and resources. | Threads share memory and resources of same process.

What Happens When You Turn On Your Computer
CPU initializes and looks for firmware (BIOS/UEFI).
BIOS performs POST (Power-On Self Test).
Hardware components like RAM and devices are checked.
BIOS then searches for a bootable device.

Bootloader Process
BIOS loads the bootloader from the storage device.
Bootloader loads the Operating System kernel.
After kernel loads, the OS starts user-space programs.
Examples: GRUB (Linux), Bootmgr (Windows), boot.efi (MacOS).

Introduction to Process
Program: Compiled code stored in disk that is ready to execute.
Process: Program that is currently under execution in RAM.
Operating System converts a program into a process before execution.
Processes allow multitasking in modern operating systems.

Steps in Process Creation
1. Load the program and its static data into main memory.
2. Allocate runtime stack for function calls and local variables.
3. Allocate heap memory for dynamic memory allocation.
4. Initialize I/O resources if needed.
5. OS hands control to the program's main() function.

Process Control Block (PCB)
PCB is a data structure used by the OS to store information about each process.
Each process in the system has its own PCB entry in the process table.
It stores important information like Process ID, state, program counter, registers and priority.
PCB helps the OS manage and track all running processes.

Context Switching
Context switching occurs when CPU switches from one process to another.
OS saves the current process state in its PCB.
Next process state is restored from its PCB.
This operation introduces overhead but allows multitasking.

Orphan Process vs Zombie Process
Orphan Process – A process whose parent has terminated but it is still running.
These processes are adopted by the init process.
Zombie Process – Process that has finished execution but still has an entry in the process table.
Occurs because parent process has not yet read the exit status of the child.

Multi-Level Queue (MLQ)
MLQ divides the ready queue into
multiple sub-queues based on process
properties like priority or type. Each
queue has its own scheduling algorithm.
Fixed Assignment
Processes are permanently assigned to a queue.
Queue-Specific Algorithms
Example: System processes (SP) use RR, Interactive
processes (IP) use RR, Batch processes (BP) use FCFS.
Fixed Priority Preemptive
Scheduling among queues is fixed-priority preemptive
(e.g., foreground has absolute priority over background).
Starvation & Convoy Effect
Lower priority processes can starve, and the convoy effect
is present.

Multi-Level Feedback Queue (MLFQ)
MLFQ allows processes to move between
queues based on their CPU usage,
separating processes by burst time
characteristics. This prevents starvation
through ageing.
Dynamic Queue Movement
Processes move to lower priority queues if they use too
much CPU time.
I/O Bound Prioritization
I/O-bound and interactive processes remain in higher-
priority queues.
Ageing Mechanism
Processes waiting too long in lower priority queues are
moved up to prevent starvation.
Flexible & Configurable
Can be tailored to specific system requirements.
